fields.title: REALITY HATES ME
fields.excerpt: A profound personal reflection on integrity, human hypocrisy, and the struggle to remain principled in an indifferent world. It explores the painful friction between personal conviction and societal contradictions, ultimately asserting that a person's true character is defined not by life's hardships but by what they consciously refuse to become.
fields.full_text:
Reality Hates Me?

By Alpha Amadu Jalloh

I have lived long enough to know that life can turn against a man without warning, without justification, and without the slightest concern for what he has sacrificed to remain standing. I have watched people rewrite the truth to suit their interests, seen loyalty treated as foolishness, and witnessed how easily a person's dignity can become the subject of another person's convenience. What troubles me is not that life has been difficult. It is the disturbing realization that sometimes the greatest punishment for being genuine is having to survive among people who have mastered the art of pretending.

I have never demanded a perfect world. I have only questioned why decency must struggle so desperately for recognition while dishonesty often enjoys the comfort of acceptance. How does a man continue believing in humanity when the very people who speak of compassion can become completely indifferent to the suffering they inflict? And that is where my argument with reality begins.

I have seen enough to understand that the world does not always punish wrongdoing or reward righteousness. Sometimes, the dishonest are celebrated while the truthful are interrogated. Sometimes, those who destroy reputations sleep peacefully while their victims spend sleepless nights trying to recover their dignity. I have reached a point where I must ask myself whether reality is against me or whether I have simply expected too much humanity from human beings.

What disturbs me is not merely the disappointment I have encountered, but the ease with which people abandon their principles when personal interests are threatened. I have learned that some individuals admire honesty only when the truth does not expose them. They praise loyalty until loyalty demands sacrifice. They speak passionately about justice until justice requires them to confront someone they love or benefit from. Such contradictions have forced me to reconsider what it means to be human and whether morality has become something people advertise rather than practice.

I do not claim perfection. I have made mistakes, misjudged situations, trusted where caution was necessary, and sometimes allowed emotion to interfere with reason. But I refuse to accept that imperfection automatically disqualifies a person from deserving respect, understanding, or fairness. There is something profoundly disturbing about a society that demands accountability from the vulnerable while manufacturing excuses for the powerful.

I have discovered that one of the loneliest experiences in life is being misunderstood by people who have already decided what they want to believe about you. You can explain yourself repeatedly, present your intentions honestly, and still discover that some minds are not searching for truth. They are searching for confirmation of their prejudices. At such moments, silence becomes both a refuge and a punishment because speaking changes nothing, while remaining silent allows falsehood to grow.

Yet I cannot pretend that every hardship has strengthened me. Some experiences have exhausted me. Some disappointments have altered the way I trust. Some encounters have made me question whether genuine compassion is becoming a rare human achievement rather than an ordinary moral responsibility. I am not ashamed to acknowledge these realities because admitting that something has wounded me does not mean I have surrendered to it.

I am more frightened of becoming emotionally indifferent than of admitting that I have been wounded. For what becomes of a man who survives cruelty only to reproduce it? What victory is there in escaping injustice if the experience transforms him into another instrument of oppression? These questions matter to me because I do not want bitterness to become my identity, regardless of how many reasons life has given me to embrace it.

Perhaps my greatest struggle is accepting that I cannot compel the world to operate according to my conscience. I cannot demand that every person recognize my sincerity, nor can I force circumstances to respect my expectations. But I can decide what my experiences will make of me. I can remain principled without becoming naive, compassionate without surrendering my dignity, and courageous without pretending that fear does not exist.

So, when I ask, "Reality Hates Me?" I am not simply expressing frustration. I am confronting the painful distance between the world as it ought to be and the world as it actually exists.

I do not need reality to favor me. I need the courage to face it without betraying myself. And if my life must remain a continuous argument between suffering and conviction, I intend to ensure that conviction is never silenced.

Because I am not merely what life has done to me.

I am also what I consciously refuse to become.

fields.subtitle: Unveiling Sierra Leone's Social Imbalance
fields.description: An earlier, foundational work examining inequality and the social imbalances that determine who enjoys opportunity, influence, recognition and prosperity, and who remains outside the circles where privilege is concentrated.

fields.subtitle: A Citizen's Conversation with Power
fields.description: A direct conversation between the citizen and those entrusted with political authority, examining leadership, democracy, accountability and the right of ordinary people to question those who govern them. Launched in Nairobi, Kenya on 7 August 2026, officiated by Professor P. L. O. Lumumba.
